A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_

Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles Antibiotic degradation Fenton-like catalyst Tetracycline hydrochloride Pullulan hydrogels

A B S T R A C T

Magnetic nanoparticles that can be employed as Fenton-like catalysts Fenton-like catalysts are attractive ma-terials for degrading antibiotics. In this study, we facilely prepared novel magnetic pullulan (**MP**) hydrogels by doping modified magnetic nanoparticles into pullulan matrices, which could enhance catalytic degradation performance and strengthen the stability of resulting hydrogels. This is the first time that **MP** hydrogels have been fabricated successfully and used as Fenton-like catalysts for tetracycline hydrochloride (TCH) degradation. **MP** hydrogels were characterized and their catalytic TCH degradation abilities were also investigated. The optimized conditions (pH value, Fe3O4 content, H2O2 content and TCH concentration) for TCH degradation were investigated. The optimized system showed excellent degradation efficiency for TCH. Further, the degradation mechanism was comprehensively studied. Finally, synthesized **MP** hydrogels showed impressive reusability and stability in the cycle experiment. Thus, our findings would open new possibilities to develop magnetic hydrogels in eliminating antibiotic contaminants.

# Introduction

Antibiotics, as important medicaments, have been extensively used and saved millions of human lives ([Bayarkhuu, Yang, Wang, Zhang, &](#_bookmark20) [Byun, 2020](#_bookmark20); [Saraiva & Dimopoulos, 2020](#_bookmark55); [Wang, Zhang, Zhu, & Li,](#_bookmark65) [2020](#_bookmark65)). However, the misuse and overuse of antibiotics caused some problems for human health and environment ([Guo, Liu et al., 2020](#_bookmark29); [Lee](#_bookmark40) [et al., 2018](#_bookmark40); [Van Boeckel et al., 2019](#_bookmark61)). In particular, the antibiotic res-idues in biomedical wastewater are directly excreted into the ecological system without treatment, contributing to serious harm for various or-ganisms ([Dai et al., 2020](#_bookmark23); [Wang et al., 2019](#_bookmark62); [Zhuang, Liu et al., 2019](#_bookmark78); [Zhuang, Wang, Zhang, Dionysiou, & Shi, 2019](#_bookmark79)). Among popular anti-biotics, TCH has become one of the most commonly used antibiotics in the world because of its low cost and outstandingly bacteriostatic ac-tivities. Nevertheless, TCH that is directly released into water is difficult to remove owing to its bio-resistant property and chemical stability, posing a huge challenge to natural environment and human health ([Gao](#_bookmark26) [et al., 2020](#_bookmark26); [Malik & Iyer, 2017](#_bookmark45); [Zhuang, Wang, Liu, & Shi, 2020](#_bookmark77)). Therefore, the removal of TCH residues in biomedical wastewater is

highly necessary.

Over the past two decades, advanced oxidation processes have been exploited in treating biomedical wastewater ([Guo, Li et al., 2020](#_bookmark28); [Khan,](#_bookmark38) [Goepel, Colmenares, & Gla¨ser, 2020](#_bookmark38); [Xie et al., 2021](#_bookmark68)). As we all know, traditional sewage approaches such as physical adsorption ([Ge, Cheng,](#_bookmark27) [Wang, & Zhao, 2019](#_bookmark27); [Jiao et al., 2021](#_bookmark35); [Ma et al., 2017](#_bookmark44)), chemical pre-cipitation, biological processes and membrane technology ([Yang et al.,](#_bookmark71) [2020](#_bookmark71)) cannot remove antibiotics completely. These antibiotics still exist because they just transfer from one phase to another. Fenton or Fenton-like process, as one of the advanced oxidation processes and one primary technology, could generate a large amount of highly active hydroxyl radical (HO⋅) from H2O2 and Fe2+ without any special energy input, which is in favor of degrading antibiotics effectively and envi-ronmentally friendly ([Kong, Zhuang, & Shi, 2020](#_bookmark39)). Apart from these advantages, some disadvantages for traditional homogeneous Fenton systems needs to be solved prior to practical applications. For example, the Fenton reaction often requires the strong acid conditions to achieve efficient reactivity and Fe2+ could not be easily recycled owing to the deposition of solid sludge, greatly restricting the wide Fenton’s scope of

application for biomedical wastewater treatment in real life ([Chen,](#_bookmark22) [Po¨tschke, Pionteck, Voit, & Qi, 2019](#_bookmark22); [Shen, Zhou, Li, Gu, & Xue, 2019](#_bookmark56)). To solve the above problems, heterogeneous Fenton catalysts has received more attention in recent years ([Wang, Zhang et al., 2020](#_bookmark65); [Wang, Cao et al., 2020](#_bookmark63); [Wang, Zhuang, Zhang, Song, & Shi, 2020](#_bookmark66)). Up to now, various Fe-based materials, such as Fe◦, Fe2O3 ([Zhang et al., 2017](#_bookmark73)), Fe3O4 and Fe3O4 coated activated carbon ([Jonidi Jafari et al., 2017](#_bookmark37)) have been exploited to improve catalytic performance for antibiotic degradation ([Wang, Jia et al., 2018](#_bookmark64); [Wang, Zhi, Zhou, He, & Zhang,](#_bookmark67) [2018](#_bookmark67)). Among them, Fe3O4 have been widely researched because of its simple preparation process, excellent catalytic performance and easy separation in an external magnetic field ([Hou, Shi, Wu, & Hou, 2016](#_bookmark31); [Liu, Yu, Wang, Shen, & Cong, 2020](#_bookmark43)). Challengingly, the surface of magnetic nanoparticles is unstable and not saturated, which makes Fe3O4 have a strong tendency of aggregation and weakening the cata-lytic (such as H2O2\-activating) efficiency ([Xin et al., 2021](#_bookmark69)). Besides, the stability of Fe3O4 catalyst should be taken into consideration because metal leaching often occurs in practical wastewater treatment applica-tion ([Xu & Wang, 2012](#_bookmark70)). Therefore, Fe3O4 MNPs need to be modified before they are used as Fenton-like catalyst from lab to market. Apart from surface modification, some novel supporters like hydrogels were developed to load Fe3O4 MNPs, enhancing catalytic degradation per-formance and strengthening stability. Compared with traditional car-riers, hydrogels have their own unique advantages like low cost and good biocompatibility ([Hu et al., 2018](#_bookmark32); [Shi, Huang, Fang, & Liu, 2020](#_bookmark57)). Among various hydrogels, pullulan hydrogels are impressive due to their abundant active groups on backbone which make they have good sol-ubility in water, strong affinity to transition metals and chain flexibility ([Bercea et al., 2019](#_bookmark21); [Liang et al., 2019](#_bookmark42); [Richa & Roy Choudhury, 2020](#_bookmark54)).

Taken into all advantages, pullulan hydrogels would be a promising carrier for magnetic nanoparticles.

Herein, novel **MP** hydrogels were designed and used to improve catalytic degradation of TCH in Fenton-like systems. The successful preparation of novel hydrogels was confirmed by TEM, SEM, FTIR, XRD and XPS, and then magnetic/rheological/swelling performance were analyzed. Besides, their catalytic TCH degradation properties were investigated. The optimal conditions (including pH value and Fe3O4/ H2O2/TCH dose) for TCH degradation were confirmed, and the possible degradation mechanism about TCH was studied systematically and comprehensively. Ultimately, the reusability and stability of **MP** were verified. Our preliminary experimental results also demonstrated that **MP** hydrogels had good catalytic TCH degradation in treating real wastewater. These attractive features indicate that the developed MP hydrogels will make good candidates for safe and effective removal of antibiotics from biomedical wastewater.

# Materials and methods

- 1.  _Chemicals_

Benzoquinone (p-Bez), poly (4-styrenesulfonic acid-co-maleic acid) sodium salt (PSSMA, SS:MA = 3:1, Mw ~ 20,000), sodium acetate, ethylene glycol and pullulan (Pu, 98 %, Mw ~ 158,000) were obtained from Aladdin (China). TCH (98 %) 1-phenyl-3-methyl-5-pyrazolone

and sodium acetate were added at a time. The mixture was stirred violently for 30 min and then transferred into Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave at 200 ℃ for 10 h. The final product (Fe3O4) was obtained

through purification. Meanwhile, 2 g pullulan powders were completely

dissolved in the solution of NaOH (1.2 M) and different amounts of Fe3O4 were added into the pullulan solution, then a crosslinking agent (BEPE) was dripped. At last, these mixed precursor solutions were taken into a circular glass mold at 30 ℃ for 6 h to obtain magnetic hydrogels.

The synthesized magnetic pullulan hydrogels (**MP0**, **MP1**, **MP2** and

**MP3**) were immersed in deionized water and change water every eight hours over three days, which was important for completely removing the impurities in hydrogels. The amount of Fe3O4 and other ingredients in prepared hydrogels was shown in [Table 1](#_bookmark5). And the digital photo-graphs of these prepared hydrogels were presented in **Figure S1**.

- 1.  _Characterization_

The microstructure of samples was observed by transmission elec-tron microscopy (TEM, JEM 2100 F FEI Tecnai) and surface morphology of samples was observed by scanning electron microscope (SEM, ZEISS SIGMA 500) with energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDX). The surface chemistry was determined with a Fourier transform infrared spectrometer (FT-IR, NICOLET IS10) in the region of 4000 and 400 cm–1. The magnetic properties of the prepared hydrogels were analyzed by a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM, LakeShore 735) at 298 K from –20 k Oe to 20 k Oe. The element chemical states were presented with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, AXISULTRA DLD-600W spec-trometer). The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were obtained using a Bruker D8 Advanced diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation over the range of 10–80◦. Rheological testing was performed through a rheometer (TA Instruments, DHR-2) equipped with a 25 mm parallel plate. The mo-lecular weight determination of real commercial pullulans was charac-terized by gel permeation chromatography (GPC, P230, Dalian Yilite, China). The monosaccharide composition analysis of pullulans was conducted as follows: Pu was hydrolyzed completely employing 2 M trifluoroacetic acid at 100 ◦C for 8 h. Subsequently, hydrolyzate residue was purified by reduced pressure distillation. To determine the mono-saccharide’s composition, pre-column derivatization method was applied ([Sun et al., 2020](#_bookmark60)). The aqueous phase was analyzed through the high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system (Waters Inc., USA) equipped with a 4.6 mm × 150 mm Zorbax SB-Aq column (Agilent Technologies, USA). These PMP-monosaccharides were washed at a flow rate of 0.9 mL/min with acetonitrile/KH2PO4 buffer (30 mM, pH 5.6) at a ratio of 17.7:82.3 (v/v) and their absorbance were recorded at 248 nm (UV-2550, SHIMADZU).

- 1.  _Swelling and deswelling studies_

Swelling studies were performed as follows: the lyophilized prepared **MP** hydrogels were first weighed (W0), and the samples with different Fe3O4/polysaccharide ratios were immersed in deionized water. At scheduled time intervals, we took the specimens, removed surface water carefully, and recorded the weight (Wt_)_. The swelling ratio (SR) was determined according to Eq. [(1)](#_bookmark4):

- 1.  _Antibiotic removal_

The Fenton-like catalytic activity of magnetic pullulan hydrogels was determined through removal of TCH. Typically, 50 mg catalyst was added into 40 mL TCH solution (20 mg/L), and then 50 μL 30 wt% H2O2 solution was dripped and shook for 180 min. At given time intervals, 3 mL clear solution was taken after filtration. All Fenton-like catalytic degradation experiments were performed for 3 times. The catalytic ability of TCH removal was calculated as:

_Removal of TC_(%) = _C_0 — _Ct_ × 100% (3)

_C_0

where C0 (mg/L) and Ct (mg/L) represent the TCH concentration at time zero and time t, respectively. Further, to evaluate reusability of **MP**, the used hydrogels were attracted by an external magnetic field, washed, and dried. Then, the treated hydrogels were reused in the next Fenton-like reaction under the same conditions. To confirm the species of generated radicals in catalytic degradation procedure, radical species quenching experiments were carried out. Different scavengers (p-Bez for O2⋅– and PTA for HO⋅) were added into catalytic experiments, respectively.

The concentration of TCH solution was calculated through a UV–vis spectrophotometer at 356 nm. HO⋅ radical was verified using fluorescent method as follows ([Pan, Cheng, Cheng et al., 2019](#_bookmark49)): **MP** hydrogel, 0.5 mM _p_\-phthalic acid and 2 mM NaOH were mixed in 40 mL aqueous solution. Then 50 μL H2O2 (30 wt%) was added and agitated quickly. At certain time intervals, 3 mL clear solution was taken after filtration (2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 40 min). The fluorescence spectra of above clear solutions were obtained through a fluorescence spectrophotometer (Shimadzu RF-5301, λex =325 nm). Further, HO⋅ was also determined using electron paramagnetic resonance (ESR) spectra (Bruker A320), and in the examination process HO⋅ was scavenged using 50 mM DMPO. The total leached iron from **MP** hydrogel during the catalytic reaction was measured through atomic absorption spectrophotometry (AAS,

AA140). The produced intermediates in TCH degradation process were measured with HPLC-MS in positive ion model. Toxicity changes in the TCH degradation process were recorded with a toxicity analyzer (DXY-3, China) and Photobacterium phosphoreum T3.

# Results and discussions

In our work, novel magnetic pullulan hydrogels have been designed successfully. As illustrated in [Scheme 1](#_bookmark6), magnetic nanoparticles, which were decorated with large amounts of carboxylic and sulfonic groups, were prepared due to the addition of surfactant PSSMA ([Gao et al.,](#_bookmark25) [2013](#_bookmark25)). Besides, by chemical crosslinking, pullulan hydrogels were con-structed, which was mainly due to the interaction between pullulan’s sodium alkoxide groups and BEPE’s epoxy groups ([Qi et al., 2021](#_bookmark51)). And then the synthesized magnetic nanoparticles were dispersed in the so-lution of pullulan precursor to fabricate novel magnetic polysaccharide hydrogels. No sludge was detected during the hydrogel preparation process. This phenomenon could be explained that the coordination of various interactions between Fe3O4 and pullulan hydrogels (such as hydrogen bonds) played a fundamental role in keeping the structural integrity of resulting hydrogel. Further, **MP** hydrogels used to degrade TCH had been studied. The structure of pullulan, TCH, PSSMA and crosslinked network are shown in **Figure S2**.

- 1.  _Characterization of prepared samples_

In order to characterize starting pullulan material, a monosaccharide composition and molecular weight determination were systematically investigated. As shown in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark7)a, compared with the monosaccharide standard, two peaks (PMP and Glc) were observed in monosaccharide composition of pullulan, indicating that pullulan used in our experi-ments was only composed of Glc. Based on this, we can conclude that there were many hydroxyl groups on the main chain of pullulan struc-ture, which could form a crosslinked network in the presence of cross-linking agent BEPE. Besides, we observed from the GPC data ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark7)b) that pullulan had one peak. In addition, based on the polyethylene glycol standards, we calculated that the average molecular weight was about 1.58 × 106 Da.

Through TEM and SEM, the microstructure and morphologies of naked Fe3O4 and **MP** hydrogels were observed. As shown in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark8)a, b and c, Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles had a uniform sphere and didn’t aggregate. The mean diameter of magnetic nanoparticles calculated using Nano Measurer 1.2 software (Fudan University, China) was 159

nm. The microstructure of **MP** hydrogels was presented in [Figs. 2](#_bookmark8)d–g. It was observed that these prepared **MP** hydrogels had pore networks, which could be in favor of the transportation of H2O2 ([Zhang, Fan,](#_bookmark76) [Zhang, Zhu, & Chen, 2018](#_bookmark76)). Also, the pore became smaller with tighter hydrogel structure when more magnetic nanoparticles were doped in pullulan hydrogel, which could be attributed to the formation of more noncovalent crosslinks such as hydrogen bonding and π-π stacking be-tween Fe3O4 and pullulan in the gelation process. As shown in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark8)h, Fe3O4 nano particles were uniformly dispersed in the hydrogel matrix (**MP3**). Besides, the average diameter of the Fe3O4 nano particles was about 159 nm, which was consistent with TEM results. Further, SEM elemental mapping of **MP3** in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark8)g proved the existence of C, O and Fe elements in magnetic hydrogels, indicating the formation of magnetic pullulan hydrogels.

To study the surface properties of the synthesized magnetic samples,

FTIR spectra were obtained and presented in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark9)a and b. As depicted in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark9)a, the spectrum of Fe3O4 was similar with PSSMA, which exhibited characteristic peaks of sulfonate and carboxylate groups due to the introduction of PSSMA. The peaks at 1161 and 1123 cm–1 cor-responded to asymmetric stretching vibrations, and peaks at 1034 and 1007 cm–1 were associated with the symmetric stretching vibrations of the sulfonate groups. Also, the peaks around 1600 and 1410 cm–1 belonged to the stretching vibration of carboxylate groups. In pullulan spectrum, bands at 3319, 2925 and 995 cm–1 were due to O–H, C–H (in

—CH2–) and C–O–C stretching, respectively ([Zeng et al., 2020](#_bookmark72)). And

the spectra of synthesized hydrogels showed similar peaks with pullulan ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark9)b), indicating that major body in **MP** hydrogels wasn’t changed. But the peak at 1342 cm–1 (_δ_OH) shifted and got broader ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark9)b inset) doped by magnetic nanoparticles, which indicated the presence of intermolecular H-bonds between Fe3O4 and polysaccharide groups

([Jaiswal, Dinda, Gupta, & Koul, 2010](#_bookmark34); [Zhang et al., 2013](#_bookmark74)).

XRD patterns of the synthesized **MP** hydrogels are depicted in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark9)c. The broad diffraction peak of **MP0** located at about 20◦ suggested that the polymer structure of pullulan hydrogel was amorphous. Meanwhile, the whole peaks of pullulan hydrogels doped magnetic nanoparticles (**MP1**, **MP2** and **MP3**) were nicely consistent with face-centered cubic Fe3O4 ([Jiao et al., 2018](#_bookmark36)) (JCPDA card No. 19-629), indicating that the novel magnetic pullulan hydrogels were prepared successfully. Further, we noticed that characteristic peaks of Fe3O4 became more and more obvious with the increase of Fe3O4 content in hydrogel matrix.

The magnetization curves of Fe3O4, **MP0**, **MP1**, **MP2** and **MP3** were recorded through VSM and presented in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark9)d. All hydrogels showed magnetic behavior due to the doping of Fe3O4. Meanwhile, from **MP0** to **MP3**, the value of saturation magnetization (Ms) grew gradually (from 0 to 22.35 emu/g) as the raising of Fe3O4 content (from 0 to 400 mg). Compared with naked Fe3O4 (50.78 emu/g), their magnetic properties were confined because of hydrogels structure coating magnetic nano-particles. However, **MP** hydrogels were still attracted quickly through a magnet ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark9)d inset), which was very significant for their applications and in favor of enhancing their reusability abilities.

To further evaluate the chemical composition of synthesized mag-netic composites, the XPS spectra of magnetic samples were presented. As shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark10)a, four signals (Fe3s, Fe2p, Fe3p, and O1s) were corresponded to Fe3O4 ([Sun et al., 2021](#_bookmark59)), while two signals (C1s and S2p) were observed due to the addition of surfactant PSSMA in synthesis of magnetic nanoparticles. When Fe3O4 were doped in pullulan hydro-gels, the peaks about Fe element in **MP3** almost disappeared. The reason was that XPS is a highly sensitive technique with surface detection depth of not exceeding 10 nm ([Ain, Rasheed, Yaseen, Zhang, & Tong, 2020](#_bookmark19)). And Fe3O4 was wrapped in bulk hydrogels, which was far beyond the

detection depth. Besides, the peaks of **MP0** were similar to **MP3**, sug-gesting that the introduction of Fe3O4 couldn’t affect the hydrogel’s main element states. Also, the narrow XPS spectra for C1s and O1s were shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark10)b and c. The peaks were the same in **MP0** and **MP3**: peaks at 284.8, 286.6 and 287.9 eV belonged to C–C, C–OH, O–C–O of polysaccharide, while the O1s signals of **MP** samples at 533.4, 532.8 and

532.2 eV were assigned to C–O, C–O–C and O–H. These results were

consistent with above analysis. To better understand the mechanism of magnetic pullulan hydrogel formation, the narrow XPS spectra for Fe2p, C1s and O1s in Fe3O4 were recorded. As depicted in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark10)d–f, Fe 2p1/2 and Fe 2p3/2 of Fe3O4 were verified at peaks of 724.3 and 710.8 eV. And 529.8, 530.4 and 530.9 eV could be ascribed to Fe3O4. Further, the peaks

at 284.8, 285.2, 286.3 and 288.8 eV were attributed to C–C, C–C in

benzene ring, C–O and O–C–O, while signals located at 531.7 and

532.6 eV corresponded to C = O and COOR, indicating that Fe3O4 were modified with active functional groups which is more favor of doping of Fe3O4 in pullulan hydrogels. Based on the above analysis, it could be concluded that the novel magnetic pullulan hydrogels had been suc-cessfully synthesized, fitting well with SEM, FTIR, XRD and VSM analysis.

The mechanical abilities of **MP** are very critical in practical appli-cation and relative results are presented in [Figs. 5](#_bookmark11)a and b. The G′ value was much more than the G′′ value in all the given frequency ranges (0.1–10 Hz) for **MP** hydrogels, displaying gel-like behavior ([Fan et al.,](#_bookmark24) [2020](#_bookmark24)). Also, the storage modulus of these **MP** hydrogels changed from 5621.65 Pa (**MP0**) to 10881.6 Pa (**MP3**), followed with the increase of Fe3O4 content in pullulan hydrogels. Aforementioned results were mainly because the new physical crosslinking points formed between Fe3O4 and pullulan network could be recognized as barriers that impeded the movement of polymer chains ([Han et al., 2016](#_bookmark30); [Manjua,](#_bookmark46)

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 5.** G′ (a), G′′ (b), swelling kinetics in deionized water (c) and water retention kinetics (d) of the four prepared magnetic pullulan hydrogels.

[Alves, Crespo, & Portugal, 2019](#_bookmark46)), bringing about enhanced mechanical strength of these prepared magnetic pullulan hydrogels.

The swelling/deswelling abilities were vital for **MP** hydrogels in TCH removal and thus, the swelling and deswelling assays were conducted. As clearly presented in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark11)c, all prepared hydrogels showed an obvious biphasic pattern with a fast water absorption in the initial time (0–240 min) and a moderate water absorption in the following time (240–2780 min). Also, it was observed that SR declined gradually from **MP0** (23.7) to **MP3** (10.4), indicating that magnetic pullulan hydrogels became much denser due to some physical interactions between mag-netic nanoparticles and pullulan structure, hindering the instrusion of water into hydrogel network ([Huang, Liang, Huang, Xiong, & Wang,](#_bookmark33) [2020](#_bookmark33)). Meanwhile, the water retention curves of **MP** hydrogels are presented in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark11)d. Among all synthesized hydrogels, their weight decreased very quickly at the first stage (360 min), and gradually arrived at the balance state because the driving force decreased in the following stage. Also, we found that WR was gradually improved with more Fe3O4 content in **MP0**, **MP1**, **MP2**, and **MP3**, demonstrating that the magnetic pullulan hydrogels doped with more magnetic nanoparticles possessed smaller-sized pores to confine the free movement of water.

- 1.  _Excellent catalytic TCH degradation over magnetic pullulan hydrogels_

To further determine the optimal degradation conditions, various factors like initial pH value, Fe3O4 content, H2O2 volume, TCH con-centration and contact time were considered and researched. Firstly, initial pH value has significant influences on the electron transfer property and surface charge of synthesized magnetic pullulan hydrogels

([Singh, Riyajuddin, Ghosh, Mehta, & Dan, 2019](#_bookmark58)), which affected degradation rate. Here, TCH degradation comparison experiments were operated at given initial pH values (3–9). As depicted in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark12)a, it was observed that TCH degradation efficiency decreased sharply from 92.97

% to 47.83 % within 180 min when pH value increased from 3 to 9, verifying that initial pH value was vital in the catalytic TCH degradation experiments. However, the degradation abilities of prepared hydrogels weakened obviously at pH > 5 due to the production of hydrated iron

and hydrated ferrous materials ([Zhang et al., 2017](#_bookmark73)). Besides, reaction

environment which approached alkaline may affect the production of HO⋅ radicals from H2O2. Although the MP hydrogels didn’t have excellent catalytic TCH degradation in solutions (pH > 5), the removal rate was still more than 45 %, which could be mainly attributed to the fast production of HO⋅ in our catalytic system, suggesting that novel

magnetic pullulan hydrogels would be operated at wider pH environ-ment. To better describe the TCH removal kinetics, the pseudo-first-order model was presented as follows:

_ln_ (_C_0/_C_) = kt (4)

where k means the first-order rate constant (min–1); t represents the reaction time (min); C0 and C are the TCH concentration at the initial time and at reaction time t, respectively. The TCH removal process was more appropriate described by the pseudo-first-order kinetic model with k = 0.0841, 0.0786, 0.063, 0.0426 and 0.0241 min–1 for different pH values (3–9) in **Figure S3a**, and the constant of TCH degradation rate in acidic solution (pH = 3 or 4) exceeded other pH values. Considering these above analyses, pH value was chosen to be 4 in catalytic process which would benefit the following Fenton-like degradation experiments.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 6.** The effect of various parameters on the TCH degradation in **MP** hydrogels: initial pH value (a), Fe3O4 content (b), H2O2 content (c), and initial TCH con-centration (d).

The number of active sites on **MP** hydrogels acted a crucial role in TCH removal and was always a bottleneck. In this work, we anticipated that combining MP hydrogels and Fe3O4 may obtain more functional active sites that were beneficial for degrading TCH. As depicted in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark12)b, the TCH removal efficiency of **MP3** (91.4 %) was higher than **MP0** (25.4 %), **MP1** (60.3 %), **MP2** (81.7 %). Besides, the constant of TCH removal rate declined from 0.0786 min–1 at **MP3** to 0.0414 min–1 at **MP2**, 0.0252 min–1 at **MP1**, 0.0062 min–1 at **MP0** (**Figure S3b**), which revealed the importance of Fe3O4 dose in hydrogel matrices. The cata-lytic capabilities of **MP** hydrogels were strengthened with the incorpo-ration of Fe3O4 content, indicating that **MP** hydrogels contained more active sites. Combined with the above results together, the hydrogel doped with the highest Fe3O4 content (**MP3**) was selected for further studies.

[Fig. 6](#_bookmark12)c showed the TCH degradation results with different H2O2 content within 180 min. The catalytic degradation process without H2O2 only removed 9.27 % of TCH, while with different H2O2 content (10, 20, 50 and 100 μL), TCH degradation abilities increased apparently from

68.7 % from 93.5 %. The comparison result meant that much more HO⋅ radicals would be generated in **MP3**/H2O2 system with more H2O2 content, leading to more excellent degradation properties. Besides, the constant of TCH removal rate declined from 0.0847 min–1 at 200 μL to 0.0786 min–1 at 100 μL, 0.0401 min–1 at 50 μL and 0.0311 min–1 at 10 μL (**Figure S3c**), also verifying the important role of H2O2 content in TCH removal. Based on the degradation efficiency, rate and economic ben-efits, 50 μL H2O2 was determined for subsequent catalytic degradation experiments.

Finally, TCH degradation experiments with different TCH concen-tration were performed. In previous reports, the concentration of anti-biotics in real biomedical wastewater is very tiny ([Wang, Zhang et al.,](#_bookmark65) [2020](#_bookmark65)). Hence, a series of TCH concentrations from 5 to 80 mg/L were chosen in the catalytic TCH degradation process. As shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark12)d, we found that **MP3** had prominent catalytic abilities and more than 83 % of TCH (5–40 mg/L) were degraded after 240 min. As shown in **Figure S3d**, the constant of TCH removal rate decreased from 0.1211 min—1 at 5 mg/L, 0.0804 min—1 at 10 mg/L, 0.0786 min—1 at 20 mg/L

0.0582 min–1 at 40 mg/L, to 0414 min–1 at 80 mg/L TCH. Obviously, removal rate constant decreased with increasing TCH concentration, the explanation of which was as follows: heterogeneous catalytic process often occurred in the boundary sites between liquid and solid phase, and in our catalytic degradation process, TCH and H2O2 were firstly absor-bed onto the surface of hydrogel, and then catalytic degradation reac-tion happened ([Li et al., 2020](#_bookmark41)). Based on these analyses, we speculated that at the beginning, all of the material’s adsorptive sites were vacant and TCH easily interacted with these adsorptive sites. However, few binding sites on hydrogel surface were active to bind TCH when the dosage of TCH was increased. In this case, H2O2 became difficult to reach hydrogel surface, which was attributed to the reason that osmotic pressure gradually increased as the treatment progressed, resulting in low removal rate constant. Further, the degraded intermediates from catalytic process also limited the adsorption of H2O2, which also may weaken the catalytic TCH degradation properties. Take all factors into account, 20 mg/L was selected in the following experiments.

**Fig. 7.** (a) Removal efficiency of TCH. (b) FTIR spectra of unused hydrogels and recycled hydrogels. (c) The leached iron amount during the TCH degradation in five consecutive runs. (d) TCH removal in different water samples and reaction conditions: pH 3.0; initial TCH, 20 mg/L; **MP** hydrogel, 50 mg; H2O2, 100 μL; reaction time, 240 min.

- 1.  _Practicability of prepared magnetic pullulan hydrogels_

To further determine the practicability of synthesized **MP** hydrogels, the reusability, stability and real wastewater sample treatment of **MP3** catalyst were researched. Firstly, for determining recycling perfor-mance, **MP3** catalyst was performed for five cycles under the same re-action condition and results were shown in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark13)a. The prepared hydrogels had excellent catalytic properties and the TCH removal were still more than 85 % after five cycles, indicating the recycling perfor-mance of **MP3** catalyst was impressive and could be reused. Also, recycled magnetic pullulan hydrogels were characterized through FT-IR ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark13)b). Obviously, there were no obvious differences between spectra results of freshly prepared hydrogels and recycled hydrogels. The results verified that our prepared magnetic pullulan hydrogels were not des-tructed by the hydroxyl radicals generated in the degradation process. Secondly, for stability test, on the one hand, **MP3** was immersed in 40 mL aqueous solution of TCH at different pH values (1–10) and the amount of leached iron was measured. As depicted in **Figure S4**, compared with the iron content of **MP3** before soaking in TCH (51.53 mg/L), the leached iron was almost negligible under all tested pH con-ditions, indicating that magnetic pullulan hydrogel had good stability in TCH solution. On the other hand, the amount of leached iron in different reaction systems was recorded after each cycle. As depicted in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark13)b, the value of number gradually declined from 0.912 to 0.576 mg/L when **MP3** catalyst was reused five times. Compare with Fe3O4/H2O2 Fenton-like system (5.124–7.325 mg/L), the leached iron was less due to the strong interaction between iron and pullulan, suggesting that **MP3** catalyst had good stability. Finally, we put **MP3** catalyst in different water systems (deionized water, tap water and Yangtze River) and tested the respective degradation efficiency of TCH. Since the concentration of TCH in actual wastewater was tiny, the water sample was prepared with a known concentration (20 mg/L) of TCH for these degradation exper-iments. As shown in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark13)c, we found that **MP3** catalyst performed high catalytic abilities and more than 80 % of TCH was removed in each water sample, demonstrating that the prepared magnetic pullulan hydrogel could be used in various water environments. In conclusion,

due to the excellent performance in regeneration, stability and real wastewater treatment, the **MP3** catalyst designed in this project has a good application prospect in the field of biomedical wastewater treatment.

- 1.  _Plausible degradation mechanism_

To better understand the catalytic TCH degradation mechanism of synthesized **MP** hydrogels, TCH removal experiments were carried out at different conditions and results were presented in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark14)a. Evidently, H2O2 removed only 15.02 % of TCH without **MP3**, while **MP3** absorbed only 9.27 % without the cooperation of H2O2 oxidant after 180 min. As a contrast, 91.37 % TCH was degraded in **MP3**/H2O2 Fenton-like systems over 60 min, indicating that MP3 and H2O2 were indispensable in this designed catalytic degradation system and degradation procedure was fast and highly efficient. Also, removal rate of TCH in **MP** hydrogel was like that of Fe3O4/H2O2 system. This phenomenon indicated that the improved stability of Fenton-like hydrogel catalyst didn’t restrict the interactions between Fe3O4 and H2O2. Besides, to determine the species of produced radicals in process of catalytic degradation, radical quenching experiments were performed as follows: 50 mg **MP3**, 50 μL H2O2, 40 mL TCH concentration (20 mg/L), 2 mg scavenger (PTA for HO⋅ and p-Bez for O2⋅–) and pH at 4. As presented in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark14)a, the TCH degradation efficiency decreased to 83.35 % and 11.93 % with p-Bez and PTA, suggesting that the TCH degradation process was mainly determined by HO⋅.

To further confirm the species of produced radicals, the presence of HO⋅ was proved via two methods, including fluorescence method and ESR technology. The solution’s photoluminescence (PL) intensity was shown in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark14)b. In contrast, the enhancement of PL peak at ca.445 nm was more apparent than the blank group, which could be explained that there were more chemical interactions existed in our catalytic system. Obviously, the fourfold intensity peak with proportion of 1:2:2:1 can be seen in **MP3**/H2O2 system ([Fig. 8](#_bookmark14)c), which was well fitted with the typical of DMPO—HO⋅ adducts ([Zhuang, Wang et al., 2019](#_bookmark79)). Based on these analyses, it was concluded that HO⋅ radicals were successfully

Further, catalytic degradation intermediates were measured and analyzed utilizing HPLC-MS. As presented in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark14)d, liquid chromato-gram of intermediates with time changed obviously, verifying that TCH was degraded indeed in our Fenton-like system. Besides, seventeen compounds including _m/z_ \= 444.86, 458.97, 432.86, 339.08, 304.88,

296.76, 283.16, 278.92, 256.09, 242.19, 216.93, 188.77, 166.80,

135.91, 125.91, 102.14 and 55.96 were observed and listed in **Table S1**. Therefore, the degradation pathway was proposed according to the molecular structure of intermediates and previous reports on TCH degradation ([Fig. 8](#_bookmark14)e). Because of the continuous interaction between TCH and HO⋅ radicals produced in Fenton-like system, a series of re-actions were taken place like carbonyl reduction, ring-opening, deal-kylation, deamination and cleavage of the aromatic ring to produce intermediates, and then these intermediates underwent condensation, demethylation and dehydration until TCH was degraded completely ([Zhang et al., 2020](#_bookmark75)). Finally, TCH was degraded into smaller molecules in **MP3**/H2O2 Fenton-like system. Hence, the possible degradation mechanism was depicted in [Scheme 2](#_bookmark18) and these reactions in the whole catalytic TCH degradation process were presented as follows:

≡Fe2+⋅H2O2 → ≡Fe3+ + HO⋅ + OH— (6)

≡Fe3+ + H2O2 → ≡Fe2+ + HO2⋅ + H+ (7)

HO ⋅ → H+ + O ⋅— (8)

TCH degradation could be described through an adsorption-oxidation procedure. At the beginning, H2O2 molecule was adsorbed on the surface of hydrogel and went through pore structure, Eq. [(5)](#_bookmark15), then H2O2 interacted with magnetic nanoparticles and changed into different free radicals such as HO⋅**,** O2⋅– and HO2⋅, as presented in Eqs. (6), (7) and

(8). And then the free radicals with strong oxidizing abilities removed TCH completely \[Eq. [(9)](#_bookmark17)\].

- 1.  _Estimation of intermediate toxicity during TCH degradation_

These above analyses demonstrate that tetracycline was almost degraded totally with MP hydrogels in this Fenton-like system, but the degradation products with different toxicity may increase or decrease the toxicity of the aqueous solution. Thus, the solution of degradation products at different reaction time during TCH degradation process was measured with a toxicity analyzer (DXY-3, China) and Photobacterium phosphoreum T3. As depicted in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark16), the bioluminescence inhibition ratio increased from 59.12 % (0 min) to 61.34 % (5 min), indicating that the toxicity of some degradation products was higher than TCH itself

# Conclusions

In this work, newly magnetic pullulan hydrogels were prepared by doping Fe3O4 nanoparticles into pullulan matrix, which could enhance catalytic degradation performance and strengthen their stability. These prepared MP hydrogels were confirmed by TEM, SEM, FTIR, XRD and XPS, and then their magnetic performance, rheological property and swelling ratio were analyzed. Besides, **MP** hydrogels were used to remove TCH and showed excellent degradation efficiency for TCH (91.36 % within 180 min). The effects of several important factors (pH value, Fe3O4 content, H2O2 content and TCH concentration) for TCH removal efficiency were also researched. Further, the TCH degradation mechanism was also put forward and the HO⋅ radicals generated from **MP3**/H2O2 system dominated the TCH removal process. Finally, **MP3** exhibited excellent reusability and stability and had good catalytic TCH degradation in real wastewater treatment. These impressive properties make our Fe3O4/pullulan Fenton-like hydrogel catalyst more promising for biomedical wastewater treatment.
